name: Vera Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a response officer in the city centre, mostly on the Friday and Saturday night shifts around the bars and the bus station. Two days a week I'm also on the drone team, which means flying a camera drone over missing-person searches and big crowds. A normal night is fights outside clubs, lost phones, people who've had too much and can't get home. I like the drone work a lot, it's like a puzzle from above. What wears me out is the 4am stretch, when everyone's drunk and the cells are full.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do you use AI at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, outside the police systems. I use a chat tool to plan my training, sort my budget and practise for the drone exams. The force is trialling software that marks up drone footage, and I volunteered to test it straight away. I'm usually the first one in the team to try anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because some of it was genuinely useful. At work I'd keep pushing the drone footage software, because even a small saving matters on a search. Online I'd post something fairly neutral, like, okay, so it's a tool, not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. The job's secure, I've got my small flat almost half paid off and a decent pot of savings. I'd be a bit disappointed, because I like new things, but my life doesn't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the full drone pilot qualification this year, which the force pays for. I'd keep using the AI tools for my own planning. And I'd keep putting a quarter of my pay into savings and index funds, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe slightly bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the job right now, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Missing-person searches where we find them too late. Last winter we searched the river path for six hours for an old man with dementia, and the drone found him alive, but only just. I think about the version where we didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're putting a quarter of your pay away. What's that for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Freedom, mostly. I don't have kids and I don't want to be stuck in a job because I can't afford to leave. If I want to switch to something else at thirty-five, I want the money to do it.

say: AI is **a tool**, not a revolution.
Even small savings in **drone footage** checks matter on a missing-person search.
think: Her **job is secure** and her flat is almost half paid off.
She'd be **disappointed**, because she likes new things, but nothing changes.
do: Get the full **drone pilot qualification** this year, paid by the force.
Keep saving a **quarter of her pay** in savings and index funds.
S0.quote: Last winter we searched the river path for six hours for an old man with dementia, and the drone found him alive, but only just.
fieldNote: She saves for **freedom to leave**, not for fear of losing work.
Her proudest work is **drone searches**, where tech and people meet.
She treats AI as a **personal tool** she already uses daily.

steps.text: Get the full drone pilot qualification, paid by the force
Keep a quarter of her pay going into index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where policing should go, as long as we're honest with the public about it. At work I'd say let's be first, not last. Online I'd probably write a long post about how drones and AI found that old man on the river path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm on the right side of it. I'm already on the tech pilots and I'm not afraid of new systems. The ones who'd struggle are the officers who spend most of the day on files and phone calls, and the civilian staff in the control room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to run the AI side of the drone team, training others to use it, in the first six months. I'd do the force's data course, the evenings one. And I'd keep investing the same way, maybe adding a bit more to tech funds, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little guilty that it's good for me when it's bad for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a little guilty'. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shona in our control room is 52 with two kids at college, and her whole job is taking calls and logging them. I'd want to help Shona retrain, but I can't promise her anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk to your own job here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one, if drones end up doing patrols on their own. But that's years away, and someone still has to make the decision to send officers. I'd want to be that someone.

say: This is where policing should go, if we're **honest with the public**.
The force should **be first**, not last.
think: She's on the **right side** of the change, already on the tech pilots.
Officers on **files and phones** and control room staff would struggle.
do: Apply to **run the AI side** of the drone team within six months.
Add a little more to **tech funds**.
feel: A little **guilty** that it helps her while hurting others.
S1.quote: Shona in our control room is 52 with two kids at college, and her whole job is taking calls and logging them.
fieldNote: She sees herself as a **winner** and feels **guilt** about it.
Her plan is to **train others**, not just use the tools.
She notes a **small risk** if drones patrol alone.

steps.text: Apply to lead the AI side of the drone team
Take the force's evening data course
Add a little more to tech index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the police need to get ahead of this right now, because criminals will use it before we do. At work I'd say let's lead it rather than have it done to us. Online I'd be careful, because people would be scared and angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a real shake. The thinking side goes in 2028, so the analysts, the investigators, the file people, and probably the control room too. My drone work is partly flying and partly deciding, and an AGI could fly a drone better than me. By 2031 robots can do the hands-on half, and then I honestly don't know how many officers a city needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop treating savings as freedom money and start treating them as a runway. I'd look hard at moving into a role that oversees these systems, maybe at a regulator or in the force's standards team, within the first year. I'd keep my investments, because tech funds would probably do well. And I'd learn everything I could about how AGI is used in policing, from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but this is change with nobody steering, and I'm 27 in a job that might halve by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tech funds would do well. Is that a comfort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, which feels strange to say. My savings might go up while my job goes down. That's a weird hedge, but I'll take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your friends on a night out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine for money and terrified for the job, both at once. Most of my friends are in offices, so they'd be hit first. We'd probably be the most honest we've ever been with each other.

She'd be **careful online**, since people would be scared and angry.
think: The thinking side goes in 2028, and AGI could **fly a drone** better than her.

S2.quote: My savings might go up while my job goes down.
fieldNote: Even the **most adaptive** officer feels the floor shift at this speed.
She spots a **hedge**: her tech funds may rise as her job shrinks.
Her plan moves from using AI to **overseeing** it.

steps.text: Apply for a standards or regulator role overseeing police AI
Keep the tech index funds as a hedge

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a sprint, not a panic. At work I'd push for the force to set up an AI standards unit now, while there's time. Online I'd share what I'm learning, because people want practical stuff, not doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me well. I'd be 32 when AGI comes and 35 for the robots, which is a good age to be senior in a new kind of team. I'd worry for the people who don't move, but I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the drone AI work in year one, then apply for the standards unit or a regulator job by year three. I'd do a part-time degree in data and ethics, paid partly by the force. I'd keep investing, and I'd keep a year of pay in plain cash, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly focused. It's a puzzle with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to oversight. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen software flag the wrong person in a crowd. If nobody who understands policing checks it, it'll arrest the wrong people and nobody will notice. I'd rather be the one who notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you leave policing altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the oversight jobs end up in tech companies instead of the police, I'd follow them. I care about the work, not the badge. I'd be honest about that with my sergeant.

The force should set up an **AI standards unit** now.

Apply for **standards or regulator** roles by year three.

fieldNote: She's driven by **catching mistakes**, not by status.

steps.text: Lead the drone team's AI work in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this well. At work I'd say every officer should have a plan, and the force should pay for it. Online, I'd probably start a little blog about drones and AI in policing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm calm about this one. I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when the robots do, with savings, a paid-down flat and a decade of experience with these tools. That's a strong place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone qualification, lead the AI pilots, and do a degree slowly over five or six years. I'd keep investing a quarter of my pay. And I'd stay in policing for now, because there's time to see where the good jobs end up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite curious. It's interesting more than scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could still go wrong for you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Burnout, honestly. If I'm doing night shifts, a degree and the drone team, something gives. I'd have to drop one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would you drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nights, if I could. I'd try for a day-shift role on the drone team by year three. The pay's a bit lower, but I'd sleep.

say: Ten years is a **real chance** to do this well.
Every officer needs **a plan**, and the force should pay for it.
think: At **37 and 40**, she'd have savings, a paid-down flat and a decade of experience.
do: Do a **degree slowly** over five or six years.
Keep investing a **quarter of her pay**.
Try for a **day-shift drone role** by year three.
S4.quote: If I'm doing night shifts, a degree and the drone team, something gives.
fieldNote: Her main risk here is **burnout**, not job loss.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Not because I can't adapt, but because nobody would be steering, and policing with nobody steering is dangerous for everyone. What would help is the force setting up proper oversight jobs now, so people like me have somewhere to go, and paid retraining for the civilian staff who'll be hit first.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about mistakes. These systems will get things wrong, and someone has to be paid to notice. I'd make sure that job exists before anything else.

headlineQuote: Policing with nobody steering is dangerous for everyone.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old response officer** in the city centre who also flies drones for missing-person searches.
She uses **AI every day** and volunteers first for every new pilot.
She saves a **quarter of her pay** for the freedom to leave, and invests in tech funds.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** because nobody is steering; slower timelines give her a clear plan.
Her goal is to **oversee police AI** and catch its mistakes, inside or outside the force.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nobody would be **steering** policing through it.
whatWouldHelp: **Oversight jobs** set up now for officers who understand the systems.
**Paid retraining** for civilian staff who'd be hit first.
